source_refs.note: 4- Population Dispersion or Distribution: a main subheading of Demography: Characteristics of Populations, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 237-237.

blocks.text: Another key characteristic of population structure is the way in which individuals of a population are dispersed or distributed within the population.

items: Random spacing: In random spacing, the individuals within populations do not interact strongly with one another. It is not common in nature. For example, it occurs in some plants that have wind-dispersed seeds that germinate wherever they fall in a favorable environment.

Uniform spacing: In some populations, individuals are uniformly distributed. For example, some plant species inhibit the growth of nearby individuals, leading to a uniform distance between each plant. Similarly, animals that maintain defined territories, such as nesting penguins, also exhibit uniform dispersion.

Clumped spacing: In some populations, individuals clump into groups or clusters due to uneven distribution of resources. Clumped spacing is common in nature because individual animals, plants, and microorganisms tend to prefer resourceful habitats. Clumped spacing is seen in plants that drop their seeds straight to the ground, or animals that live in groups.
